Sten-throsis is the formation of a thrombus on the sub-endothelial collagen that is exposed by a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque. Virchow's triad states that thrombi form due to alterations in 3 factors:1) The integrity of the vessel wall - due to atherosclerosis creating a rough surface for the adhesion of platelets2) The composition of blood - due to increased thrombin (thrombin is an enzyme that catalyses the final step of clot formation: prothrombin to thrombin) which makes blood hyper-coagulative3) Blood flow - disturbed flow allows clotting factors and platelets to come into contact. These 3 factors can lead to thrombosis, the formation of a clot that occludes the lumen of a blood vessel. This can lead to MI if the vessel is a coronary artery.

Dendritic cells share a lot of similarities with macrophages so far this question writer is personally going to be kept at arm's length. However, the main difference is that Dendritic cells are the only antigen presenting cells that are able to migrate from the site of infection to the nearest draining lymph node. Whilst they are in the lymph node they interact with naïve T cells and give them a boost (via B7) to expand their immune response. They also present the peptides taken up by the endosomal compartment in the dendritic cell on their MHC (Dendritic cells can have two types of MHC, MHC I and II). Macrophages do not migrate to the nearest lymph node and they cannot present A/B cell receptors (although they can present MHC II).
